• Other names: Congo frog, African Dwarf Frog, West African clawed frog, ADF, DAF
  • Tank size (optimal): 5 gallons (~20 litres)
  • Keeping: easy to medium; breeding: medium to difficult
  • pH: 6.5–7.5; GH 5–20; KH 4–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: carnivore / omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful (with caution)
  • Colour: from olive green to greyish and brown

When choosing these frogs at the pet store, make sure they are healthy and active. They should at least swim away or try to hide when the staff fish them out. A sick frog is slow to respond, whereas a healthy frog will dive and seek cover quickly.

All new frogs should be quarantined for a minimum of 30 days before any interaction with current frogs, to reduce the risk of spreading disease.

Be careful in pet shops: African clawed frogs (Xenopus laevis) look similar when small, and some shops sell them as dwarf African clawed frogs. The two must never be mixed. Xenopus laevis is a voracious predator and cannibalistic, and will massacre other fish, shrimp and frogs in a community tank.

Taxonomy: Hymenochirus has only 4 recognised species: H. boettgeri, H. boulengeri, H. curtipes and H. feae. They look much alike and are hard to separate even for scientists. H. boettgeri and H. curtipes can interbreed, so some breeders believe most frogs in the trade are hybrids. H. curtipes looks similar to H. boettgeri but has wartier skin; claimed differences such as slightly larger size, fewer spots, greyer colour and more forward-facing eyes have not been scientifically proven. Pet stores often use the same names for all of them.

Important: recent studies suggest that, because of increased demand for rainforest wood, the whole Hymenochirus genus may become extinct in its native range in the near future.
Hymenochirus curtipes is native to the Congo basin of central Africa. It is mostly found in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo.
The dwarf African frog is restricted to shallow, thickly vegetated swamps, ponds, sloughs, ditches and other marshy wetlands surrounded by shaded tropical forest. It prefers stagnant water.

The minimum recommended tank for a pair is 5 gallons (~20 litres). The tank should let the frogs move or swim around, turn fully in any direction without obstruction from the walls, and avoid contact with tankmates when needed.

A larger tank is always preferable for water stability: in small tanks everything can go wrong so fast there is no time to fix it, and larger tanks also leave room for environmental enrichment.

These frogs come from shallow waters, so do not use tall tanks, as they are stressful and the frogs are poor swimmers. Ideally the water should be no more than 25–30 cm deep. They need long, not tall, tanks to breathe air at low energy cost.

Although fully aquatic, they have been known to leave the water, so a secure lid is safer. An escaped frog that is not returned to the water in time dehydrates and dies quickly. If they keep trying to get out, check the water parameters.

Do not add frogs to an uncycled tank. High ammonia and nitrates quickly kill them because they absorb moisture through the skin. A stable nitrogen cycle is the most important factor, and they cannot tolerate ammonia and nitrites.

Dwarf African clawed frogs are very messy and need clean water. Water should be completely dechlorinated before use: chlorine destroys their protective mucous layer and can predispose them to pathogens. Let water age for 24 hours; chlorine evaporates within 24 hours, though larger volumes can take longer (about 48 hours for a large volume) and some chlorine may remain.

If you use tap water, beware of heavy metals. The water system should not be galvanised or copper, as copper ions released by corrosion can kill the frogs.

  • Remove chlorine, chloramine and contaminants before adding water to the tank.
  • Do water changes every week of 20–30%.
  • Do not use distilled or RO water without remineralising it first.
  • Use a water conditioner, for example Seachem Prime, which also detoxifies gases and binds heavy metals, ammonia, nitrites and nitrates for up to 48 hours.

Molting: they shed their skin every two to three weeks, rubbing against surfaces to speed it up. Leave the shed skin, as they eat it, but remove it if it is still in the tank after 24 hours, otherwise it fouls the water.

Quarantine every new addition (plant or tankmate) before adding it to the tank. New frogs should be quarantined for a minimum of 20–30 days.

Handling: these are not pets to play with. Handling harms their tender skin and can lead to infection or death. Never lift them by the legs. Do not touch them with bare hands unless there is no option; hands must then be absolutely clean and wet, since any residue (soap, lotion) is absorbed through the skin. Ideally use gloves, but not powdered or textured ones. If you must transfer them, a soft net may be used (nets are generally not recommended), with the opening covered, taking care that delicate hands and legs do not get tangled. Out of water, their porous skin can cause fatal dehydration within 15–20 minutes. Do not touch frogs from different aquariums with the same gloves, as infection can be transferred.

Health hazard for humans: Hymenochirus frogs are a potential source of Salmonella infection. Do not let small children touch the frogs, use gloves, wash hands thoroughly after contact, and do not clean tank equipment (nets, feeding dishes) in sinks where food is prepared.

If you buy captive-bred frogs, find out the water parameters they were bred in, as they may be accustomed to less ideal conditions. If you cannot find out, presume the breeder kept them close to natural conditions and replicate those.

  • Temperature: 23–26 °C.
  • pH: 6.5–7.5.
  • Hardness: they do not like very soft water; 5–20 GH and 4–12 KH.
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm.

Stable water conditions are essential; poor environmental conditions are the leading cause of stress, and any change must be made very gradually, even changes for the better.

Heaters and other electronic elements should be hidden or placed out of the frogs' reach. A thermometer is useful for tracking the water temperature.

Filtration and water flow: they prefer still or slow-moving water, while bubble filters and aeration cause disturbance and vibrations that stress them. Because of their clumsiness, they can also get stuck in intakes. Recommended:

  • Cover intakes with sponge.
  • Choose filters with adjustable flow (set as low as possible for the tank).
  • If you use a mechanical filter, use sponge filters so the frogs are not blown away.
  • Aim the output at a corner.

Substrate: bare bottom, gravel or sand can be used.

  • Bare bottom: safe and easiest to clean (a turkey baster removes waste and uneaten food), but not attractive, and it does not replicate their natural habitat and will eventually stress them.
  • Gravel: must be large enough that the frog cannot eat it, since swallowing gravel causes intestinal blockage and death. Use smooth gravel without sharp edges to reduce the risk of skin lacerations.
  • Sand: generally the most favourable. It looks more natural, is safer and easier to clean, and frogs that swallow it often spit it out, so the risk of injury is limited.

Lighting: no special requirements. They are nocturnal and do not depend on light; 8–10 hours of light is enough. If you keep plants, adapt the lighting to the plants.

Decorations and hiding places: provide plenty, as they are very skittish. Hiding places reduce stress, which is especially crucial during molting when the frogs are weak and vulnerable. They appreciate leaves, rocks, driftwood, PVC pipes, plastic mesh, plants and other decorations. Artificial plants are an alternative to live plants; thicker plants give many good hiding spots.

In the wild they are relatively non-specific predators and scavengers, feeding preferentially on aquatic insects and worms, scavenging decaying debris, and may even resort to cannibalism, eating their own tadpoles.

In captivity they readily accept daphnia, brine shrimp, cyclops, bloodworms, blackworms, Tubifex worms, chopped earthworm, trout and similar foods. Any fish or shrimp food (pellets, tablets, flakes) will do as long as it sinks. Raptomin sticks are an excellent basic commercial food.

  • Freeze-dried or dehydrated food may make them bloated; if so, switch to live food for a week or so. Bloodworms should be given no more than 1–2 times a week as a treat, as they are high in fat and can cause bloat or obesity.
  • A small ceramic dish for feeding keeps the substrate clean.

Feeding is one of the most problematic parts of keeping them, as they are slow and inefficient eaters. They are almost blind and rely on smell and water vibrations, so they are poor at finding food. In a community tank they often end up underweight or starving because fish find the food first, which is another reason species-only tanks are recommended.

How often: adults typically eat once a day, 3 or 4 times a week; do not be afraid to fast them. Juveniles should be fed daily or at least 5–6 times a week, as they need more food to grow. If food is not eaten within 30 minutes to an hour, remove it and try again a few hours later; uneaten food causes water problems.

How much: as much as they can consume in 10–15 minutes. Avoid overfeeding, which is harmful and clouds the water.

Variety: do not give the same food for weeks; change the diet at least every few days.

Fasting: they can reduce their metabolic rate, so adults can easily go a few days without food. Do not give a huge feeding after fasting; give the usual amount.

Hymenochirus curtipes is naturally nocturnal. Activity peaks at dusk and gradually stops before sunrise, mainly to avoid visual predators while feeding.

They are rather lazy frogs and do not move much during the day, usually hiding or resting at the bottom or top of the tank. They like to stand on their hind legs with the nose out of the water or simply float at the top. As long as they eat well and show no skin problems, they should be fine.

They are social and prefer to be kept in a group or at least as pairs. They are very peaceful and not aggressive, although smaller frogs are occasionally bullied by larger ones. Males squawk (a quiet buzz or hum) to find a mate, which is normal.

They are shy, prefer to swim away when somebody approaches, and need lots of hiding places. They are not good swimmers and can drown if they cannot reach the surface. They need permanent water but have been known to leave it occasionally; moribund frogs preferred a terrestrial environment.

Life span: there is no data for wild individuals. In captivity they regularly live 5–6 years, and with appropriate care up to 8 years.

Description: small, completely aquatic frogs. Adults can reach up to 7 cm, though the average is 4–5 cm snout-to-vent. The skin is damp and slippery thanks to mucous glands that form a protective barrier against pathogens and damage; it also acts as a respiratory membrane, reduces water loss and helps regulate body temperature. They sense their surroundings by smell, touch and motion through the water, with lateral lines across the body that detect changes and movements and help them find food. Their hearing is well developed. The eyes are lidless, circular and flat, and the frogs are almost blind, mostly reacting to shadows. They have lungs, not gills, so they must obtain oxygen at the surface, as skin respiration is not enough. They lack both teeth and a tongue despite being carnivorous.

Tankmates: although peaceful, social and small, a species tank is highly recommended because they are carnivores and will act on instinct. Feeding is also difficult if the tank has active bottom-dwellers.

  • Fish: they will try to eat anything that fits their mouth, so any fish under 2.5 cm can be eaten; do not keep them with small tetras, guppies, gouramis, etc. Large, nippy or aggressive fish (goldfish, cichlids, puffers, etc.) should also be avoided. Compatibility with bettas is individual: some bettas harass the frogs, but there are also reports of them being great companions.
  • Dwarf shrimp: not good tankmates, they will eventually all be eaten. Larger species such as Amano and ghost shrimp, growing to about 5 cm, have a chance to survive.
  • Snails: the frogs may sometimes eat baby snails or snail eggs; otherwise they usually leave freshwater snails alone, as hard shells discourage them.
  • Bad tankmates: large or aggressive fish, crayfish, crabs and turtles. The frogs are too small and weak to fight back and will quickly end up as food.

Hymenochirus curtipes shows obvious sexual dimorphism:

  • Size: fully grown females are larger than males (by around 30%) and pear-shaped as their abdomens fill with eggs near mating. Males are skinnier.
  • Tail: females have a small tail between the legs.
  • Breeding glands: males have a red, whitish or grey pimple near each armpit. These breeding glands enlarge during sexual activity and secrete pheromones to attract females.
  • Noise: males "sing" or "hum" with a zippy or buzzing noise, frequently in the evening and at night, to attract females.

Hymenochirus will repeatedly produce eggs only when all conditions are right, so breeding is rare without some effort. According to some observations, to stimulate breeding they should be kept in water no deeper than 10–15 cm; they usually stop breeding in deeper water.

Maturity and mating: females usually mature at roughly 9 months, males at about 1 year. Males secrete chemicals that stimulate females, and receptive females are attracted to any advertising male. The male clasps the female just above her rear legs as she swims (amplexus), which stimulates hormonally primed females to expel eggs. Mating can last a few hours, often a single night, sometimes longer. The female lays eggs at the water surface and the male fertilises them as she does so.

Eggs: larger females produce more eggs. Females do not lay all eggs at once, and in general may produce from a few hundred up to 1500 eggs. Under optimal conditions eggs hatch within 1–2 days (about 24 hours).

Tadpoles: free-swimming life lasts about 27 days. Fully grown tadpoles reach about 2 cm before transforming into frogs. They are entirely carnivorous and, due to their small size, need micro-organisms in the first few days.

The frogs are cannibalistic and eat their own eggs and tadpoles, so remove the eggs and raise the young separately.

Dwarf African clawed frogs are not hard to care for once their needs are understood and a routine is established. They are cute but not very active. The great majority of problems can be traced back to poor feeding, inadequate water parameters and tank maintenance.

Name: German zoologist Oskar Boettger originally named them African dwarf clawed frogs for the small black claws on their hind legs. These claws are generally lost as the frogs mature, so they are now more commonly called dwarf African frogs.

Diseases and infections are not rare:

  • Bloat (dropsy): caused either by internal bacterial infections, which are almost always fatal, or by abnormal accumulation of body fluids due to improper metabolism, which is not lethal. Draining with a needle is not recommended, as it can damage an organ and the problem usually returns. Treatment: a salt bath of one teaspoon of sea salt or non-iodised salt per about 4 litres, no more than 20 minutes per day until cleared.
  • Red leg: red lesions and swelling on the hind legs are a sign of the bacterium Aeromonas hydrophila. Other signs include muscular spasms, lethargy and vomiting. Once it reaches the blood the animal will not survive. Treatment: oral tetracycline 1 mg per 5 g body weight for 5 days, or salt at 100 mM plus 100 micrograms per ml oxytetracycline in the water for a week with daily water changes. Isolate infected animals and all they had contact with, and disinfect all nets and tanks.
  • Fungal infections: often go hand in hand with bacterial infections, caused by skin infection with Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis. Signs include anorexia, lethargy, skin pigment changes, loss of the slime layer and death. The skin thickens, disrupting electrolyte balance, and it is usually fatal. Treatment: Mardel Maroxy anti-fungal solution, also effective against some bacteria.

If a frog shows problems, remove it to a separate tank, consult professional vets or the Association of Reptile and Amphibian Veterinarians. With several frogs, move the infected one immediately to a hospital tank.
